# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
# Review: Reduced Working Time at Full Pay (Halden WP 24-07)

The arithmetic is internally consistent. Every per-hour figure equals the output index divided by 0.8. The employee-weighted mean of 98.7 reproduces from the sector rows. Counts and headcounts sum correctly, and the percentage changes in Table 2 match their inputs.

The problems are in what the numbers are taken to show. The headline productivity result is largely produced by how it is calculated, the sector-general conclusion is contradicted by the paper's own data, and the limitations section underrates biases that all point the same way.

## 1. The output-per-hour gain is mostly arithmetic

"Output per scheduled hour" is the output index divided by 0.8. Any organisation whose index stays above 80 will show a per-hour gain, and an index near 100 will always show roughly +20–25%. So:

- **"Gains in output per hour in every sector" adds no evidence.** It was nearly guaranteed once hours were cut by 20% and outputs were reported near baseline.
- **"Size and consistency" can't support the main result.** The Limitations section relies on them, but the size comes from the 0.8 divisor, and the consistency follows from every index landing between 93 and 101.
- **The informative number is the output index.** The question is whether output was maintained. Overall it fell 1.3%; in retail and hospitality it fell 6.9%.
- **Pay was unchanged, so cost per unit of output rose.** It rose about 1.3% overall (100/98.7) and about 7.4% in retail and hospitality (100/93.1). The deal promised "100% of the output"; retail delivered 93%.
- **The denominator is scheduled hours, not actual hours.** The paper admits actual hours weren't collected (Limitation 4). Any work done on the day off, longer remaining days, overtime, or extra staff hired to maintain coverage shrinks the true per-hour gain. Headcount changes aren't reported at all.

I'd recommend leading with "output was 98.7% of baseline (93.1% in retail)" and treating the per-hour figure as derived, with that caveat attached.

## 2. The data contradict "sector-general"

- **Retail and hospitality is the weakest case, not a confirming one.** It had the lowest output (93.1), and 3 of its 6 organisations reverted. That is a 50% reversion rate, against 0 of 50 in the four knowledge-work sectors.
- **Healthcare administration was similar.** 2 of 5 organisations reverted.
- **Continuation contradicts the Discussion.** The Discussion calls the high continuation rate "itself evidence." By that same standard, the revealed preference in customer-facing sectors goes against the sector-general claim.
- **The sample is thin and skewed.** Retail and hospitality is 6 organisations and 300 staff. "Healthcare administration" is not clinical healthcare. There is no manufacturing, logistics, education, construction or clinical care. Eighty-seven percent of staff are in office or knowledge-work sectors, which are exactly the sectors the paper says the view is wrong about.

The defensible conclusion is roughly: output was broadly maintained in professional, IT, media and non-profit organisations; results in customer-facing sectors were weaker, and half of those organisations reverted.

## 3. The primary outcome is weak, and its biases all point one way

- **Self-assessment by the people running the pilot.** The output index is completed by the managers responsible for the pilot. They used "whatever output records the organisation held," with no standardisation or audit.
- **Anchoring.** The scale anchors "100 = unchanged," and the bargain everyone signed up to was 100% output. Even a modest optimistic bias of a few points is larger than the 1.3% shortfall being interpreted.
- **Seasonality isn't controlled.** The baseline is the six months *before* the pilot, so the primary outcome isn't adjusted for seasonality. Revenue is compared year-on-year precisely to remove seasonality, so the paper applies the fix to its secondary outcome but not its primary one.
- **Selection compounds this.** All of the following push results toward success:
  - organisations volunteered;
  - the 9 that withdrew "chiefly for scheduling reasons" were excluded, though these are plausibly the ones that found it unworkable;
  - interviews cover 58 of 61 organisations;
  - revenue covers 52 of 61.

  An intention-to-treat framing would count the 9 withdrawals; at minimum, report what is known about them.

The closing claim that the limitations are "unlikely to overturn the main result" is not justified. The main result is a 1.3% difference measured by interested parties without a control group.

## 4. Revenue is weaker than presented

- **+1.4% is nominal.** The paper doesn't say where the pilot ran, but in most economies 2023 inflation was well above 1.4% (roughly 4–7% across the US, eurozone and UK). A nominal +1.4% probably means a real decline.
- **Missing data may not be random.** Nine organisations didn't report revenue, and the paper doesn't say which.
- **The weighting is odd.** Employee-weighting revenue growth is unusual and isn't explained.
- **There is no comparison with sector trends.**

"Offers no sign that output was sacrificed" overstates the case. At best, revenue is uninformative.

## 5. Wellbeing and retention results have mechanical and timing components

- **Sick days fall partly by construction.** On a four-day week, a sickness falling on the day off isn't recorded. Exposure alone falls about 20% (4.4 × 0.8 = 3.5), which accounts for over half of the reported 36% drop. Report sick days per scheduled day.
- **Seasonality could affect sickness too.** If the baseline included winter months and the pilot didn't, the effect would be inflated. Recruitment in early 2023 plus two months of preparation suggests exactly that pattern.
- **Resignations are annualised from six months during an active perk.** Staff have reason to stay at least until the outcome is known. Labour-market conditions aren't controlled.
- **Energy is fading.** It rose 0.61 SD at month 3 but only 0.29 SD at month 6, roughly halving in three months. That pattern looks like a novelty effect. It bears directly on the duration limitation and undercuts the fatigue explanation, yet the Discussion doesn't mention it.
- **The productivity self-rating has no baseline.** "64% rate own productivity higher" is a retrospective self-report. Survey response rates and sample sizes aren't reported anywhere.

## 6. The causal explanation isn't supported

The paper calls reduced fatigue "the most plausible single explanation," but fatigue was never measured against output. The paper's own interview evidence instead points to process changes:
- fewer meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58 managers),
- protected focus blocks,
- simpler approvals.

Managers called the schedule a "forcing device" for changes they had wanted for years. Those changes could plausibly be made without cutting hours, which matters for anyone deciding whether to adopt the policy. The paper should either drop the fatigue claim or present it as one hypothesis alongside process change.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Mixed weighting.** The summary mixes employee-weighted outcomes with organisation counts (92% continuation) without flagging the difference.
- **Coverage arrangements are undocumented.** Seventeen organisations used staggered days off to maintain coverage. How was this done: overtime, temps, new hires? This matters most for the customer-facing results.
- **Quality isn't measured.** There are no measures of service quality or customer outcomes, which matter most in retail, hospitality and healthcare administration.
- **Some useful facts are buried.** "18 made it permanent immediately" is mentioned without saying which sectors those organisations were in.
- **Withdrawal timing is unclear.** If any withdrawals happened after scheduling had been trialled, they bear on feasibility.

## Suggested reframing of the Summary

> Sixty-one volunteer organisations, mostly in knowledge-work sectors, cut scheduled hours by 20% at full pay for six months. Manager-reported output averaged 98.7% of the prior six months (93.1% in retail and hospitality), without a control group or measurement of actual hours. Organisations reported lower sickness absence and resignations. 92% continued, but half of the retail and hospitality organisations reverted. Results support further controlled trials, particularly in customer-facing sectors, rather than a sector-general conclusion.

I can draft revised Summary, Discussion and Limitations sections, or a short list of analyses to request from the authors (actual hours, sick days per scheduled day, the withdrawn organisations, real revenue).
